metaDescription: White Hall sits in Marion County's coal-and-gas overlap. We trace the deed record, check split-estate history, and buy mineral interests.
heroLead: White Hall's mineral history runs through both coal and gas, and untangling which estate you actually own often means reading two different kinds of severance deed on the same tract.
intro: Marion County's mineral history covers more than gas alone. This was Consol Energy coal country for generations, and it's common to find a White Hall tract where the coal seam was severed from the surface by one deed and the oil and gas rights were severed separately, sometimes decades apart and to different parties entirely. Sorting out which estate a family actually still holds is often the real work behind a White Hall mineral sale.

We pull the Marion County deed record to confirm exactly what was severed, when, and to whom, before we ever discuss a number. A tract's coal history doesn't determine its gas value, but the two are frequently tangled together in the same chain of title and need to be read apart.

sections.heading: Marion County's Coal-and-Gas Overlap
paragraphs: Much of Marion County's mineral estate was split into layers well before the Marcellus era — coal severed first in many cases, with oil and gas reserved or conveyed under separate language, sometimes in the same deed and sometimes years apart. That layered history means a White Hall owner may hold the gas rights while a different party altogether owns the coal, or vice versa.
We read the full severance history on a White Hall tract rather than assuming a single clean mineral estate, because assuming wrong there produces a wrong offer.

sections.heading: White Hall's Split Estate Reality
paragraphs: It's routine here to find a surface owner who has no mineral rights at all, a coal owner unrelated to either, and a gas interest held by a third party or split among several heirs. None of those three groups necessarily know what the others hold.
If you're not sure whether your family owns coal, gas, or both under a White Hall tract, that uncertainty is common and it's exactly what we sort out first.

sections.heading: Flat-Rate Leases From the Coal Era
paragraphs: Some of the gas leases still on file for Marion County tracts near White Hall date back decades, written as flat-rate agreements before the county saw meaningful Marcellus interest. If a modern well has since been drilled under a unit covering one of these tracts, West Virginia's statutory 1/8 royalty floor generally requires that lease to convert.
We check the lease and any nearby well activity before we value a gas interest, because an old flat payment and a converted royalty interest are worth very different amounts.

sections.heading: Heirship on Small Marion County Tracts
paragraphs: Family tracts around White Hall were often small to begin with, and generations of inheritance have split some of them into undivided fractions held by more heirs than the original acreage would suggest. We've bought interests here representing a small fraction of a small tract, still worth pursuing once the ownership was properly traced.
We handle that tracing directly through the Marion County record and buy from individual heirs without requiring the full family group to participate.

faqs.question: How do I know if my family owns the coal, the gas, or both under our White Hall property?
faqs.answer: We trace the Marion County deed record to confirm exactly what was severed and to whom, which tells us specifically which estate, if any, your family still holds.

faqs.question: Does an old coal lease affect the value of our gas rights?
faqs.answer: Not directly — the two estates are typically valued separately — but confirming the severance history matters because it tells us exactly what you own before we make an offer.

faqs.question: Our old gas lease pays a small flat amount every year. Is that normal?
faqs.answer: It's common on older Marion County leases from before the Marcellus era. Whether it should have converted to a royalty depends on nearby well activity, which we check as part of valuing the interest.
